This report delivers a technical and legal audit of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program, provincial and territorial research and development (R&D) tax credits, direct innovation funding instruments, administrative compliance protocols, and judicial precedents in Canada as of November 2026.

The Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most significant structural expansion in over a decade with the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and for depreciable property acquired or lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (yielding up to $2.1 million in annual refundable federal cash credits on current expenditures), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs that had been repealed since January 1, 2014. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a voluntary Pre-Claim Approval process offering upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks.

At the sub-national level, provincial responses to the federal Bill C-15 reforms have diverged across Canada. British Columbia (via BC Budget 2026, tabled February 17, 2026) expressly aligned with the federal reforms—doubling its 10% refundable credit expenditure limit to $6 million, adopting the $15 million–$75 million phase-out range, extending refundability to ECPCs, restoring capital expenditures, and permanently removing its statutory expiry date. Conversely, Quebec replaced five legacy R&D tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 with the unified, refundable Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) (announced in the 2025–2026 Québec budget as the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization) (offering 30% on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold, and 20% thereafter). Ontario retained its $3 million cap on the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) while updating provincial ministry guidance to recognize post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures, Alberta maintained its independent $4 million cap under the permanent Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), and Saskatchewan increased its 10% refundable CCPC threshold from $1 million to $2 million.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Structure under the Income Tax Act

Canada's federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Program—originally introduced in 1944 as an immediate deduction for current scientific research expenses and structured in its modern dual-incentive form since 1985—operates through two distinct, sequential statutory mechanisms under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA). Together, these two provisions allow qualifying taxpayers both to deduct eligible R&D outlays from taxable business income and to earn a volume-based investment tax credit that reduces federal Part I tax payable or generates a direct cash refund.

The first statutory mechanism is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under Section 37 of the ITA. Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current expenditures and—for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024—allowable capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada. This expenditure pool permits the taxpayer to deduct up to 100% of unclaimed allowable SR&ED expenditures against business income in the current taxation year or carry any undeducted positive balance forward indefinitely to shelter taxable income in future taxation years.

The second statutory mechanism is the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA. Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), a taxpayer earns an ITC calculated as a statutory percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of their net "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at year-end. Non-refundable ITCs reduce Part I federal income tax otherwise payable and may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years, while qualifying taxpayers may claim a direct cash refund of unused ITCs under Section 127.1.
The statutory interaction between Section 37, Section 127, Section 248, and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (Sections 2900 to 2903) follows a strict three-step legal sequence:

items: Step 1 (Activity Eligibility — Subsection 248(1)): Determine whether the scientific or technological activities meet the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA and do not fall within the excluded work categories in paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k).

Step 2 (Allowable Deductible Expenditures — Section 37 & Regulations 2900(2)–(3)): Determine whether the outlays linked to the eligible work constitute allowable current or capital SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) and subsection 37(8), computed under either the Traditional Method or the Proxy Method.

Step 3 (Qualified Expenditures for ITC Purposes — Subsections 127(9), 127(11.1)–(11.8), 127(18)–(20) & Regulations 2900(4)–(11), 2902): Convert allowable SR&ED expenditures into "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) by adding the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (if elected) or Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) amounts, applying the 80% statutory inclusion rate to arm's-length Canadian contracts and third-party payments, excluding prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902 and payments to non-taxable suppliers, and deducting all government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments.

body.text: 1.2 Historical Evolution and the Statutory Definition of SR&ED in Subsection 248(1)

The legislative definition of SR&ED has evolved through a series of statutory and regulatory amendments designed to distinguish genuine scientific or technological advancement from routine commercial engineering. Prior to 1985, administrative guidance under Interpretation Bulletin IT-439 struggled to clarify the scope of eligible development. In 1963, Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations introduced the formal concept of "scientific research" as a systematic investigation or search carried out in science by experimentation or analysis to acquire new knowledge or devise new or improved products or processes, and in 1967 Regulation 2900 was amended to categorize basic research, applied research, and development alongside direct support work. Following the May 23, 1985 federal budget papers, subsection 2900(1) of the Regulations was amended in 1986 (effective May 23, 1985) to introduce the title "scientific research and experimental development" (SR&ED), replacing the word "development" with "experimental development" to exclude projects involving only routine engineering or routine development.

On March 4, 1986, the Department of Finance confirmed to Revenue Canada that qualifying R&D must embody scientific or technological advancement, involve scientific or technological uncertainty, and be carried out in a systematic and organized fashion. That same year, Revenue Canada and industry leaders developed Information Circular 86-4 (later revised as IC 86-4R3 in 1994, alongside Interpretation Bulletin IT-151R5-CONSOLID on SR&ED expenditures), establishing the three foundational criteria of scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and scientific and technical content. In 1995 (applicable to taxation years ending after December 2, 1992), Regulation 2900(1) was amended to define experimental development explicitly as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement and to expand paragraph (d) support work to eight specific categories subject to a dual test: being "commensurate with the needs" and "directly in support" of basic research, applied research, or experimental development. The definition reference was added to subsection 248(1) of the ITA in 1996 (for work performed after February 27, 1995), and in 1998 the substantive definition was moved directly into subsection 248(1) of the ITA, adding the explicit requirement that paragraph (d) support work be undertaken "in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer". On June 26, 2013, Royal Assent was granted to amend the French version of paragraph 248(1)(d) to replace "travaux techniques" with "travaux de génie" to ensure consistency with the English term "engineering".

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "scientific research and experimental development" means systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls into one of four eligible categories while avoiding seven statutory exclusions:

cells: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.
Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes.
Research in the social sciences or the humanities (which disqualifies projects rooted in social, economic, or behavioural analytics rather than natural or applied sciences).
Prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas.
The commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process.

body.text: 1.3 Mechanics of the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Subsection 37(1) of the ITA establishes a cumulative, running expenditure pool calculated at the end of each taxation year. Per the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy (updated March 27, 2026), positive balances in the Section 37(1) pool do not expire and may be carried forward indefinitely to be deducted against business income in any subsequent taxation year.

The pool is increased each year by six statutory additions under subsection 37(1). First, paragraph 37(1)(a) adds expenditures of a current nature on SR&ED carried on in Canada, encompassing SR&ED directly undertaken by the taxpayer (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)), contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the taxpayer (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), third-party payments to Canadian-resident corporations to be used for SR&ED in Canada related to the claimant's business (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)), third-party payments to approved associations, universities, colleges, research institutes, or granting councils (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii) and clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(E)), and payments to tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)). Second, paragraph 37(1)(b) adds allowable capital expenditures incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada—a provision that was repealed for property acquired from January 1, 2014 to December 15, 2024, and restored under Bill C-15 for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024. Third, paragraph 37(1)(c) adds repayments of government or non-government assistance that had previously reduced the pool. Fourth, paragraph 37(1)(c.1) adds amounts included in the taxpayer's taxable income in a previous year under paragraph 12(1)(v) (which occurs whenever year-end reductions to the Section 37 pool exceed additions, driving the pool negative). Fifth and sixth, paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and 37(1)(c.3) add amounts included in Part I tax payable in the prior year due to direct or partnership SR&ED ITC recapture. Pool balances transferred on a qualifying corporate amalgamation or wind-up are also added.

Conversely, the Section 37(1) pool is reduced by six statutory deductions. Under paragraph 37(1)(d), the pool is decreased by all government assistance and non-government assistance (as defined in subsection 127(9)) that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year. Under paragraph 37(1)(d.1), provincial super-allowance benefit amounts are deducted. Under paragraph 37(1)(e), the pool is reduced by the amount of federal SR&ED ITCs applied to reduce Part I tax and/or refunded as cash in the preceding taxation year—which is the statutory mechanism that renders used or refunded SR&ED ITCs taxable in the following year. Under paragraphs 37(1)(f) and 37(1)(f.1), amounts deducted from the pool in preceding years or deducted for insolvency under section 61.3 are subtracted. Finally, under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1), if a corporation undergoes a loss restriction event (an acquisition of control) or a trust gains a new majority-interest beneficiary, the Section 37(1) pool is reduced to nil at that time and subject to streaming restrictions, though it may be reinstated in a subsequent taxation year if statutory continuity-of-business conditions are met.
Three special rules further govern the scope of Section 37:

items: Exclusive Economic Zone (Subsection 37(1.3)): SR&ED work performed in Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone is deemed to be carried on in Canada.

SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2)): Under subsection 37(2), expenditures for research carried on outside Canada are generally excluded from the Section 37(1) pool and cannot earn ITCs. However, under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), permissible salary or wages for employees performing SR&ED work outside Canada may be included in the Section 37(1) pool and earn ITCs, subject to a statutory limit (commonly referred to as the 10% foreign-travel/wage allowance, enacted following the Tax Court decision in LGL Ltd. v. The Queen, 96-4726(IT)G, 1999).

Partnerships (Paragraph 96(1)(e.1) and Subsection 127(8)): A partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37(1) pool balance to a subsequent taxation year; the entire pool balance must be deducted in computing the partnership's net income in the year incurred. Moreover, under subsection 127(8), SR&ED ITCs allocated to members of a partnership are restricted to the 15% basic rate, overriding the 35% enhanced CCPC rate (as confirmed in All Colour Chemicals Ltd. v. The Queen).

body.text: 2.2 Entity Qualification Rules: CCPCs and ECPCs

Eligibility for the enhanced 35% ITC rate and immediate cash refundability depends on whether the corporate claimant qualifies throughout the taxation year as either a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) or, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC).

To qualify as a CCPC, a corporation must satisfy four cumulative conditions at the end of the taxation year. First, it must be a private corporation resident in Canada (either incorporated in Canada or resident in Canada since June 18, 1971). Second, it must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (including both de jure voting control and de facto factual control under section 256 of the ITA), by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations, or by any combination thereof. Third, it must not be controlled by a Canadian-resident corporation whose shares are listed on a designated stock exchange outside Canada. Fourth, no class of its capital stock may be listed on a designated stock exchange.

To qualify as an ECPC under subsection 127(9) of the ITA (as enacted by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), a corporation must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year, be a "public corporation" under the ITA (or a corporation that would be a public corporation if the phrase "designated stock exchange in Canada" were read as "designated stock exchange"), not be controlled directly or indirectly by non-residents, and satisfy statutory control test requirements. Eligible subsidiaries of such public corporations also qualify as ECPCs.
2.3 Mathematical Formulas for the $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Phase-Outs

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the baseline expenditure limit on which a qualifying CCPC or ECPC (or associated/consolidated group) can earn the enhanced 35% ITC is $6,000,000. If the corporation has a short taxation year (fewer than 365 days), the expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365: Expenditure Limit × (number of days in the taxation year ÷ 365).
2.3.1 Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula for CCPCs (Subsection 127(10.2))

Unless a CCPC elects to use the revenue-based phase-out structure under subsection 127(10.31), its $6,000,000 baseline expenditure limit is phased out linearly when the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated corporations (under subsection 256(1)) is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. The statutory formula for the expenditure limit is: Expenditure Limit = Baseline Limit × [(Phase-Out Range − A) ÷ Phase-Out Range].

Under Bill C-15, the Baseline Limit is $6,000,000, the Phase-Out Range is $60,000,000 (spanning from $15,000,000 to $75,000,000), and A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 (i.e., $6 million × [($60 million − A) ÷ $60 million]). Consequently, the expenditure limit is reduced by $1 for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 and is completely eliminated at $75,000,000. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the baseline limit was $3,000,000 and the phase-out range was $40,000,000, spanning from $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital.)
2.3.2 Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula for ECPCs and Electing CCPCs (Subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.62))

For ECPCs—and for CCPCs that file an election under subsection 127(10.31) to use gross revenue instead of taxable capital—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out when average annual revenue over the three preceding fiscal years is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Using the same linear formula ($6 million × [($60 million − R) ÷ $60 million]), R represents the excess of the three-year average annual gross revenue over $15,000,000 (up to $60,000,000), eliminating the enhanced limit at $75,000,000.

For consolidated ECPC groups (subsection 127(10.62)), the single $6,000,000 limit is shared among group members that prepare consolidated financial statements (as defined in subsection 233.8(1)), using the total annual revenue from those consolidated statements. Where a CCPC is associated with other CCPCs, all associated CCPCs must jointly elect to use the revenue method, and the calculation aggregates the financial statement revenues of all group members for the three preceding fiscal years (including each corporation's reasonable share of partnership and trust revenues, with reasonable adjustments such as eliminating intra-group sales to reflect a single economic entity).
2.3.3 Associated Group Allocation and Anti-Avoidance Rules

Under subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3), associated CCPCs must share the single $6,000,000 expenditure limit by filing Schedule 49 (T2SCH49) (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026). Under subsections 127(10.22) and 127(10.23) (and parallel refundability provisions in subsections 127.1(2.2) and 127.1(2.3)), specific deeming rules allow corporations that might otherwise be associated in narrow technical circumstances to be deemed not associated, whereas subsection 256(2.1) empowers the CRA to deem corporations to be associated as an anti-avoidance measure.
2.4 Refundability Matrix and the Qualifying Income Limit (Section 127.1)

Whether an earned SR&ED ITC is refunded as cash under Section 127.1 or restricted to offsetting Part I tax payable depends on the claimant's legal entity status, whether the expenditure falls within or above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, and whether the expenditure is of a current nature or a capital nature.

Specifically, a CCPC with SR&ED spending above its $6,000,000 expenditure limit can receive a 40% partial cash refund on its 15% basic ITC only if it meets the definition of a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2)—meaning its prior-year taxable income (aggregated across all associated corporations) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Qualifying Income Limit is calculated as $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if the associated group's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount of prior-year taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the formula was $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A was prior-year taxable capital exceeding $10,000,000 up to $40,000,000.)

body.text: 3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Subsections 37(8) and 37(10))

Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA, every SR&ED claimant must elect on Form T661 for each taxation year whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). Most claimants elect the Proxy Method because it removes the need to specifically identify, track, and allocate individual overhead and other indirect expenditures. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base under Regulation 2900(4). Conversely, the Traditional Method requires the claimant to identify, track, and justify every incremental overhead expense on Line 360 of Form T661, which is advantageous when a company incurs substantial incremental overhead or cloud computing costs that exceed 55% of its internal Canadian SR&ED salary base.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages (CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy)

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the ITA. This includes regular wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips and gratuities, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, bonuses (for non-specified employees), and taxable benefits under section 6 of the ITA (such as automobile benefits, housing/board/meals, gifts and awards, interest-free or low-interest loans, group term life insurance policies, and taxable tuition fees).

Conversely, four categories of employment-related costs are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages under both the Proxy and Traditional methods. First, the employer's share of related benefits (such as employer contributions to pension plans, employment insurance, or non-taxable benefit plans) cannot be claimed as salary or wages. Second, amounts for extended vacation or sick leave are excluded. Third, under subsections 143.3(2) through 143.3(5) (enacted after Alcatel Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2005 TCC 149), employee stock option benefits and share issuances are excluded. Fourth, retiring allowances (defined in subsection 248(1) and taxed under subparagraph 56(1)(a)(ii)) are excluded from direct SR&ED salary or wages, although a retiring allowance may qualify on Line 360 as an overhead and other expenditure under the Traditional Method if it is directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED.

Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV)), only the portion of salary or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada is eligible. "Directly engaged" refers to hands-on work determined by the tasks performed rather than the employee's job title, and includes technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the year (such as assigning technological personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, and assessing the quality of materials used).

For a "specified employee"—defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who is a specified shareholder owning 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation (or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer—strict statutory caps apply under subsections 37(9) through 37(9.5). Under subsection 37(9), SR&ED expenditures never include a bonus or remuneration based on profits paid or payable to a specified employee. Furthermore, under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages that may be claimed for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual was a specified employee. Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (subsections 37(9.2)–(9.4)), the 5 × YMPE limit must be allocated among the associated corporations by filing Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) together with a certified copy of the directors' resolution on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline; otherwise, the specified employee's salary or wages are deemed not to be an SR&ED expenditure.

Finally, under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any salary or wages accrued in a taxation year that are not paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year, and can only be claimed in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (reported on Line 315). Permissible salary or wages for employees performing SR&ED work outside Canada are governed by subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5).
3.3 Overhead: The 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Overhead
3.3.1 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(4))

A critical audit verification point is the exact rate of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated April 28, 2022), the PPA rate was 65% up to 2012, 60% for 2013, and has been 55% of the salary base since 2014. Claiming a 65% proxy rate on a 2025 or 2026 filing is a statutory error that overstates the proxy overhead by 10 percentage points.
Computing the PPA in Part 5 of Form T661 requires applying two sets of statutory restrictions to the proxy "salary base":

items: Exclusions from the Proxy Salary Base (Regulation 2900(9)): Under subsection 2900(9) of the Regulations, taxable benefits under section 6 of the ITA, bonuses, and profit-based remuneration (even for non-specified employees) are excluded from the salary base to which the 55% rate applies.

Specified Employee Proxy Salary Base Caps (Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8)): Under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Regulations, the proxy salary base for a specified employee is capped at the lesser of 75% of total time/salary spent on SR&ED and 2.5 times the YMPE (shared across associated corporations).

body.text: The resulting 55% PPA (reported on Line 820 in Part 5, Section B of Form T661) is a purely notional amount included in "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) to earn SR&ED ITCs. It is never added to the Section 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.
3.3.2 Traditional Method Overhead and Cloud Computing Costs (Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3))

Under the Traditional Method, no PPA is calculated. Instead, per the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022), the claimant claims actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the ITA and Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3).

To qualify as "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada under paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations, an expenditure (or a reasonably allocated portion thereof) of a current nature must satisfy two mandatory tests. First, under the "Directly Related" Test, the expenditure must proceed directly—without an intervening step or intermediary—to link to (1) the SR&ED work, (2) the SR&ED staff, or (3) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED. Second, under the "Incremental" Test, the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Fixed costs that the business would have incurred regardless of SR&ED (such as fixed maintenance contracts or base monthly telephone and internet fees) fail the incremental test, whereas identifiable long-distance charges or incremental cloud computing expenses incurred specifically for SR&ED can qualify under the Traditional Method.

Under subsection 2900(3) of the Regulations, expenditures directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada include two components. First, costs for the maintenance and upkeep (general care, repair, and preservation) of premises, facilities, or equipment used for SR&ED are explicitly permitted based on the proportion of SR&ED use without requiring separate proof of the incremental test. Second, other expenditures (or portions thereof) under paragraph 2900(3)(b) must be both directly related to the provision of those premises, facilities, or equipment and incremental (meaning they would not have been incurred had those premises, facilities, or equipment not existed).

Even under the Traditional Method, Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations excludes "prescribed expenditures" from qualifying for ITCs, including general administration or management of a business (subparagraph 2902(a)(i)), legal or accounting fees (clause 2902(a)(i)(B)), interest expenses (clause 2902(a)(i)(C)), conventions and conferences (clause 2902(a)(i)(F)), and the acquisition of rights in or arising out of SR&ED (paragraph 2902(c)).
3.4 Subcontractors and Third-Party Payments (80% Inclusion Rule, NAL Rules, and Form T1263)
3.4.1 Arm's-Length Canadian SR&ED Contracts (80% Inclusion Rate)

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA (as detailed in the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy and Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, updated May 22, 2026), when a claimant engages an arm's-length contractor to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is included in the Section 37(1) pool of deductible expenditures, and 80% of the eligible contract expenditure is included in "qualified expenditures" for ITC calculation (enacted in 2012 to remove the profit element from arm's-length third-party contracts).

To qualify for the 80% ITC inclusion, the contract work must be performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf, and the payment must be made to a "taxable supplier" (excluded if paid or payable to or for the benefit of a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier, such as a foreign contractor without a Canadian permanent establishment). Under subsection 127(26), unpaid contract expenditures at year-end are excluded from qualified expenditures until the taxation year in which they are actually paid, at which point 80% of the amount paid is added. Furthermore, while contract expenditures between 2014 and December 15, 2024 had to be reduced by any non-current (capital) expenditure of the performer under former subsection 37(14), contract expenditures and third-party payments incurred after December 15, 2024 are generally no longer reduced by capital expenditures of the performer.
3.4.2 Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) Contracts (Subsections 127(11.6) and 127(13) & Form T1146)

Where a claimant (payer) enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer (per section 251 of the ITA), paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) provides that the payer's contract outlay is an allowable deductible expenditure in the Section 37(1) pool, but is not a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own SR&ED expenditures and qualified expenditures, and the amount received from the NAL payer is not treated as a "contract payment" that would reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures. Alternatively, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and NAL payer may file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) to transfer qualified expenditures from the performer (reported on Line 540 of Form T661) to the payer, subject to subsection 127(11.6) non-arm's-length cost rules that eliminate intercompany profit.
3.4.3 Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), (iii) & Form T1263)

Under the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy (updated March 30, 2022), a claimant may claim 100% in the Section 37(1) deductible pool and 80% in the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for third-party payments (direct financial contributions, funding of students/employees, or payments in kind valued at fair market value) made for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the claimant, where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED. Claimants must complete and attach Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment.
The CRA categorizes eligible third-party recipients into five main classes (Entities A to E, alongside Entity F for paragraph 149(1)(j) basic/applied research):

items: Entity A (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)): Corporations resident in Canada (tax incentives are earned in the year the SR&ED is performed);
Entity B (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)): Approved associations (earned in the year paid);
Entity C (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii)): Approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or similar institutions (earned in the year paid);
Entity D (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii)): Non-profit SR&ED corporations resident in Canada and exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j) (earned in the year paid); and

Entity E (Clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(E)): Approved organizations (granting councils)—specifically the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council—that make payments to a B, C, or D entity (earned in the year paid).

body.text: 3.5 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and ITC Recapture

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method) and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations (Traditional Method), as explained in the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), a claimant may claim 100% of current expenditures for materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

For an item to qualify as "materials for SR&ED," it must satisfy the CRA's tangible object requirements: the raw materials, substances, or other items must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a tangible "thing" on which the SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED. Items that do not compose the body of the thing—such as broken or used lab supplies (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes), cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, and general utilities (water, electricity, oil, natural gas)—do not qualify as materials for SR&ED, though they may qualify as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method. Moreover, the cost of materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED, not when purchased or removed from inventory.

The distinction between materials consumed and materials transformed governs exposure to ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA. Materials consumed are materials that were destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED (such as absorbed or used-up reagents or parts destroyed during testing), and they are not subject to ITC recapture. Materials transformed are materials incorporated into a prototype, custom product, commercial asset, or experimental production run (ED+EP) that were not destroyed or rendered virtually valueless.

Per the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, when a claimant disposes of or converts to commercial use any property on which an SR&ED ITC was earned—including materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), or physical property acquired through an SR&ED contract (excluding intellectual property)—within the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36)), the recapture rules add to Part I tax payable the lesser of:

items: The SR&ED ITC originally earned in respect of the particular property; and

The historical ITC rate (35%, 15%, or 20% prior to 2014) applied when the ITC was earned multiplied by either (a) the proceeds of disposition of the property (if disposed of to an arm's-length person) or (b) the fair market value (FMV) of the property (if converted to commercial use or disposed of to a non-arm's-length party).

body.text: If a component is manufactured in-house, recapture applies only to the cost of acquired materials incorporated into the property sold or converted to commercial use, and not to the internal salaries or overhead incurred to manufacture the part. Any ITC recaptured in a taxation year is added back to the Section 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2).
3.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)
Bill C-15 restored SR&ED deductibility and ITC eligibility for capital property and equipment leases acquired or incurred after December 15, 2024:
3.6.1 All or Substantially All (ASA) Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III))

Per the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), new or used depreciable property acquired and available for use (subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024 qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure if, at the time of acquisition, it satisfies the Intent Test: the claimant intended either that (1) the property would be used during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time over its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, or (2) all or substantially all (≥90%) of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada.

Non-depreciable property (land, inventory, goodwill) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings are excluded under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e). Under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) is also excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures. Any SR&ED capital expenditure deducted from the Section 37(1) pool in calculating taxable income is deemed to be an amount allowed as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), preventing duplicate CCA claims on Schedule 8 (T2SCH8).
3.6.2 Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9) & Regulation 2900(11))

Per the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA intent test may qualify for SR&ED ITCs on Line 504 of Form T661 as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) if it is actually used primarily (>50% and <90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada. Used property, GPOEF, and Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (such as property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for commercial manufacturing or for the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial plant or line) are excluded.

Under subsection 127(9), the qualified expenditure for First-Term SUE (evaluated from the date available for use until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time) is deemed to be 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost of the equipment. If the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE and continues to be used primarily (>50%) for SR&ED during the Second Period (from acquisition until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition), an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies as Second-Term SUE. The capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37(1) pool; it is depreciated under regular CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any SUE ITC applied or refunded reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the subsequent taxation year.
3.6.3 Restored Equipment Lease Expenditures (CRA Lease Expenditures Policy, June 8, 2026)

Per the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 to lease equipment used in SR&ED qualify under distinct rules for the Proxy and Traditional methods. Under the Proxy Method, if leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used ASA (≥90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), 100% of the lease cost is eligible; if used primarily (>50% to <90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), 50% of the lease cost is eligible; and if used 50% or less of the time, 0% is eligible. Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used ASA (≥90%) for SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)), 100% is claimed as a lease cost; if used <90% of the time for SR&ED, the lease cost is claimed on Line 360 as overhead proportional to the actual percentage of SR&ED use, provided it is directly related and incremental under Regulation 2900(2)(c).

In both methods, lease costs for buildings (rent) are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(e) unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building approved by Finance Canada under Regulation 2903. While desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, photocopiers, telephones, cell phones, and calculators constitute GPOEF (excluded under the Proxy Method), computers (including hardware, software, and ancillary equipment) are not considered GPOEF and therefore qualify under both methods.
4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal Stacking

Nine provinces and Yukon provide R&D tax credits on top of the federal SR&ED ITC, while Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a statutory SR&ED income tax credit. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the federal ITA, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are classified as "government assistance" and reduce both the federal Section 37(1) pool of deductible expenditures and the federal qualified expenditure pool.
4.1 Quebec: The Modernized CRIC Regime (Tax Years Beginning After March 25, 2025)

For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the Government of Québec (Information Bulletin 2025-6) replaced five legacy R&D tax credits—(1) the R&D salary credit under section 1029.7 (formerly Form RD-1029.7), (2) the university/public research centre credit under section 1029.8, (3) the private partnership pre-competitive research credit, (4) the research consortium fees credit, and (5) the technological adaptation services credit—with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation), codified under sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Taxation Act (Quebec).

Administered by Revenu Québec (with the CRA performing the scientific review of R&D eligibility), the CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit to eligible corporations with an establishment in Québec at a rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the corporation's exclusion threshold, and 20% on qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 tier. The mandatory exclusion threshold deducted before applying the credit rates is equal to the greater of $50,000 and the sum of the corporation's R&D employees threshold and pre-commercialization employees threshold.

The Québec CRIC expenditure base is computed separately from the federal base (with no Prescribed Proxy Amount) and includes 100% of eligible Québec R&D and pre-commercialization salaries and wages, 50% of payments to Québec subcontractors (compared to 80% federally), 50% of payments to eligible Québec public research centres, research consortia, or university entities, and 100% of capital property/equipment acquisition costs for eligible activities in Québec (subject to a special recovery tax if the property ceases to be used solely in Québec within 730 consecutive days following the start of its use). Crucially, where activities continue R&D carried out in Québec, the CRIC also covers pre-commercialization activities—specifically (1) tests, technological validations, and studies to meet regulatory requirements and obtain an initial registration, approval, or certification for commercializing an innovation, and (2) product design (including form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and material selection). The CRIC is claimed within 18 months of fiscal year-end with the Québec CO-17 corporate tax return using Form RD-1029.8.CR-T, Form RD-1029.8.PR-T (pre-commercialization component), and Form RD-1029.8.EN-T (associated group expenditure limit agreement).
4.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC
Ontario offers three corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) (Section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007, Schedule 566 / T2SCH566, and Schedule 5 Line 468): Provides an 8% refundable tax credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum $240,000 annual refund). Ontario has not adopted the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit; the $3,000,000 limit is shared among associated corporations and phases out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or when prior-year specified capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Per official Ontario Ministry of Finance guidance updated October 30, 2026, OITC qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (though as of mid-2026, the CRA's general OITC summary page still only referenced 100% of current expenditures). Under subsection 96(14), a corporation may waive the OITC in whole or in part.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) (Sections 38–45 of the Taxation Act, 2007, Schedule 508 / T2SCH508): Provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (reduced first by the amount of any OITC and OBRITC claimed), with no expenditure cap. Unused ORDTCs can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, or waived in writing.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC): Provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures paid to an Eligible Research Institute in Ontario, up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (maximum $4,000,000 annual refund).

body.text: 4.3 British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, and Territories

In British Columbia, BC Budget 2026 (tabled February 17, 2026) expressly aligned the BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Income Tax Act (British Columbia), sections 97–103, claimed on Form T666) with the federal Bill C-15 reforms effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. British Columbia increased its 10% refundable expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (up to $600,000 refundable), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs, restored capital expenditures as qualifying BC expenditures, and permanently removed the credit's statutory expiry date. Expenditures above the $6,000,000 limit or incurred by other corporations earn a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward).

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (Alberta Corporate Tax Act, sections 26.95–26.99)—which replaced the former Alberta SR&ED credit in 2021 and was made permanent in the 2025 Alberta Budget—is administered independently by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA). The IEG provides an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (the average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the previous 2 taxation years) and an enhanced 20% refundable payment (8% base + 12% incremental) on eligible Alberta R&D spending above the 2-year base, up to an annual expenditure cap of $4,000,000 (maximum $800,000 annual grant). The IEG phases out over $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital and is claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 within 15 months after the corporation's filing due date.

In Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit (The Income Tax Act (Saskatchewan), sections 63–63.4, Schedule T2SCH403) was expanded for qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, doubling the 10% refundable CCPC expenditure limit from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 (up to $200,000 refundable), while providing a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward) on expenditures above $2,000,000 or for non-CCPCs, up to a combined annual cap of $1,000,000 in total credits.

In Manitoba, the Manitoba R&D Tax Credit (The Income Tax Act (Manitoba), section 7.3, Schedule T2SCH380) provides a 15% credit on eligible current and depreciable capital expenditures (excluding buildings and leasehold interests in buildings) with no expenditure cap; 50% is refundable (7.5%) and 50% is non-refundable (7.5%, 3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward) for in-house R&D, or 100% refundable (15%) when conducted under contract with a qualifying Manitoba research institute. Finally, Nova Scotia (section 41, T2SCH340), New Brunswick (section 59, T2SCH360), Newfoundland and Labrador (section 42, T2SCH301 / Form T1129), and Yukon (section 15, T2SCH442 / Form T1232) each provide a 15% fully refundable tax credit (plus an additional 5% refundable credit in Yukon for payments to Yukon University, totaling 20%).

body.text: 4.5 Mathematical Demonstration of Combined Federal-Provincial Credit Grinding

Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance under subsection 127(18) of the federal ITA, the provincial credit earned in a taxation year must be deducted from the federal qualified expenditure pool before multiplying by the 35% or 15% federal ITC rate.

To illustrate the exact mechanics in Québec, consider the benchmark scenario from R&D Tax Academy where a qualifying Québec CCPC incurs $1,200,000 in Québec R&D salaries and $200,000 in payments to a Québec subcontractor, has an assumed Québec exclusion threshold of $100,000, and has $2,000,000 in federal qualified expenditures before deducting the Québec credit. First, on the Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T, the eligible CRIC expenditure base before the threshold is $1,200,000 (salaries at 100%) plus $100,000 ($200,000 subcontractor at 50%) = $1,300,000. Subtracting the $100,000 exclusion threshold leaves $1,200,000 of expenditures above the threshold. The CRIC pays 30% on the first $1,000,000 ($300,000) and 20% on the remaining $200,000 ($40,000), yielding a total refundable Québec CRIC of $340,000. Second, on the federal Form T661, deducting the $340,000 CRIC as government assistance from the $2,000,000 federal qualified expenditure base leaves $1,660,000, which at the 35% enhanced federal rate produces $581,000 in refundable federal ITC—for a combined cash refund of $921,000.

To illustrate Ontario and British Columbia under the Proxy Method (55% PPA), suppose a qualifying CCPC incurs $1,000,000 in direct arm's-length SR&ED salaries, generating a $550,000 PPA and $1,550,000 in gross qualified expenditures. In Ontario, the 8% refundable OITC yields $124,000 ($1,550,000 × 8%), reducing the base for the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC to $1,426,000 and generating $49,910 in ORDTC ($1,426,000 × 3.5%). Both Ontario credits reduce the federal qualified expenditure base to $1,376,090 ($1,550,000 − $124,000 − $49,910), yielding $481,631.50 in 35% refundable federal ITC and $655,541.50 in total combined credits (or $623,100 in all-cash refunds if the non-refundable ORDTC is waived under the Taxation Act, 2007). In British Columbia, the 10% refundable BC SR&ED credit yields $155,000 ($1,550,000 × 10%), reducing the federal qualified expenditure base to $1,395,000 and generating $488,250 in 35% refundable federal ITC, for a total all-cash refund of $643,250 (64.325% of the direct salary outlay).
5. Direct Government R&D Grants, Clean Economy ITCs, and Stacking Rules
5.1 Statutory Treatment of Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(11.1), and 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA (as detailed in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy), all government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year must be netted against SR&ED expenditures on a project-by-project basis.

Under subsection 127(9), "government assistance" encompasses any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or other form of assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and indirect funding channeled through non-profit entities), other than the federal SR&ED ITC. As demonstrated in CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2022), even government loans related to SR&ED can be treated as government assistance that reduces the SR&ED pool. "Non-government assistance" is defined in subsection 127(9) by reference to paragraph 12(1)(x) as any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance received from a non-governmental entity for the cost of property or an outlay or expense. "Contract payments" are amounts paid or payable by an arm's-length taxable supplier for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of that customer. However, as established in Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (96-4343-IT-G, 1999), a fixed-price commercial contract to deliver a product where the vendor bears the financial and technical risk is treated as commercial revenue rather than a purchase of SR&ED that grinds down the vendor's SR&ED claim.

When a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance, paragraph 37(1)(c) adds the repaid amount back to the Section 37(1) pool of deductible expenditures, and paragraphs 127(9)(e.1) and (e.2) allow the claimant to earn an ITC on the repayment at the historical ITC rate that applied when the assistance originally reduced the claim. However, because repayments are not defined as "qualified expenditures," the ITC earned on a repayment is non-refundable (it may only reduce Part I tax payable, carry back 3 years, or carry forward 20 years).
5.2 Optimizing the Stack: NRC IRAP + SR&ED + Provincial Tax Credits

The National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) is Canada's premier direct R&D grant program. According to Canadian grant advisory sources, NRC IRAP provides non-repayable, pre-approved cost-shared contributions for R&D labour and Canadian subcontractors—with the Industrial Technology Advisor (ITA) setting the cost-share percentage case by case, covering up to 75% of eligible project costs (up to $350,000 for standard SME projects and up to $10,000,000 for large initiatives).

Stacking NRC IRAP with SR&ED creates a powerful financial leverage effect under the Proxy Method because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4) is calculated on the full, unreduced eligible SR&ED salary base before the NRC IRAP grant is deducted as government assistance under subsection 127(18). For example, if a qualifying Ontario CCPC incurs $100,000 in direct arm's-length SR&ED salaries and receives a $60,000 (60%) NRC IRAP grant, its 55% PPA is still calculated on the full $100,000 salary base ($55,000), producing $155,000 in gross qualified expenditures before assistance. Deducting the $60,000 NRC IRAP grant leaves $95,000 in net qualified expenditures, which generates $7,600 in 8% refundable Ontario OITC ($95,000 × 8%) and $30,590 in 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC (($95,000 − $7,600) × 35%)—for a total cash recovery of $98,190 ($60,000 IRAP + $7,600 OITC + $30,590 SR&ED), covering 98.19% of the $100,000 wage outlay.
5.3 Other Federal Innovation Programs and Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits
Canadian R&D claimants frequently coordinate SR&ED with other federal and regional funding instruments, all of which must be tracked for government assistance grinding under subsection 127(18):

items: Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC): Challenge-based federal grants for Canadian SMEs with no matching funds required, offering up to $150,000 under Phase 1 (feasibility) and up to $1,000,000 under Phase 2 (prototype development).
Clean Technology Investment Tax Credit: Provides a refundable federal tax credit of up to 30% on eligible clean technology equipment.

AI, Sectoral, and Regional Innovation Programs: According to Canadian grant advisory sources, common co-claimed programs include the Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative (RAII) (up to $5,000,000 interest-free repayable funding covering up to 50% of eligible costs, or non-repayable streams in the Prairie provinces), Scale AI (reimbursing up to 40% of eligible AI adoption/commercialization expenses), the AI Compute Access Fund, the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) (for scale-up projects over $10,000,000), NSERC Alliance Grants, PrairiesCan Business Scale-up and Productivity (BSP) ($200,000 to $5,000,000), the Student Work Placement Program (SWPP), CanExport (up to $50,000 per project), and the Regional Tariff Response Initiative (RTRI) (up to $3,000,000 non-repayable and up to $20,000,000 total funding in Southern Ontario).

body.text: 6. Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Audit Protocols
6.1 Institutional Governance

The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers both the technical review and financial audit of the federal SR&ED program and eight provincial/territorial R&D tax credit programs (Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon), while the Department of Finance Canada oversees legislative policy under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations. Revenu Québec (alongside the Ministère des Finances du Québec) administers the Québec CRIC—relying on the CRA for the scientific review of R&D activities—and Alberta Treasury Board and Finance (Tax and Revenue Administration / TRA) administers the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG).
6.2 Structural Walkthrough of Form T661 (Updated May 15, 2026) and Ancillary Forms

To access federal SR&ED incentives, a claimant must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15, 2026 for Bill C-15) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, updated May 22, 2026) for corporations or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) for individuals and trusts. Claimants using tax preparation software to file electronically must not submit duplicate paper copies of Form T661.
Per the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and the May 15, 2026 Form T661 update notices, Form T661 is structured into 10 mandatory parts:

6.3 Statutory Filing Deadlines and the Absolute Bar on Extensions

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date:

items: Corporations (18 Months): Under paragraph 150(1)(a), a corporation's T2 filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year; adding 12 months yields a strict 18-month reporting deadline after the end of the taxation year. (For tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j), the reporting deadline is their 6-month return due date under subsection 149(7).)

Trusts (15 Months): Under paragraph 150(1)(c), a trust's T3 filing-due date is 90 days after its taxation year-end; adding 12 months yields a 15-month reporting deadline after the end of the taxation year.

Individuals (17.5 Months): Under subparagraph 150(1)(d)(ii), the T1 filing-due date of an individual who carried on a business in the year is June 15 of the following year; adding 12 months yields a 17.5-month reporting deadline after the December 31 year-end for sole proprietors.

body.text: There is no statutory mechanism to extend or waive a missed SR&ED reporting deadline. Under subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA (applicable on and after November 17, 2005), ministerial discretion under subsection 220(2.1) cannot be exercised to waive prescribed forms or prescribed information for SR&ED, and taxpayer relief under subsection 220(3.1) applies only to penalties and interest. Under paragraph 230(4)(b), all supporting books and records must be retained for six years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate.
6.4 Voluntary Pre-Claim Approval (Launched April 1, 2026), CRA Review Process, Penalties, and Appeals

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a voluntary Pre-Claim Approval process through My Business Account. Businesses may apply before starting work or incurring R&D costs, and the CRA provides a formal pre-claim eligibility decision within eight weeks. Per the CRA's The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), if a claim containing pre-claim approved projects is selected for post-filing review, the CRA may conduct an expenditure-only review, which is generally processed within 90 calendar days of receiving the complete claim (unless the executed work differed significantly from the pre-approved application or unapproved projects were included).

For standard post-filing claims, complete claims accepted without review are generally processed within 60 calendar days, and refundable claims selected for review are subject to a 180-calendar-day service standard (which the CRA commits to meeting 90% of the time), while non-refundable claims selected for review have no service standard. The normal reassessment window is 3 years from the original Notice of Assessment for CCPCs and 4 years for non-CCPCs. Once selected for review, an SR&ED claim cannot be withdrawn. Reviews are conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates work eligibility, interviews technical staff, conducts virtual or on-site tours, and prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report under a Research and Technology Manager / RTM) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who audits financial ledgers, contracts, and assistance under a Financial Review Manager / FRM). If downward adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a Proposal Package granting the claimant 30 days to submit written representations.

Under subsection 163(2) of the ITA and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), if the CRA proves (subsection 163(3)) that a claimant made a false statement or omission knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, the penalty is the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (paragraph 163(2)(a)) and (2) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed (paragraph 163(2)(d)).
To resolve disputes, claimants follow a three-step administrative process during the review:

items: Step 1: Discuss concerns directly with the RTA and/or FR.
Step 2: Escalate to the RTM and/or FRM.

Step 3 (Administrative Review — Form RC532): Before the file is closed and before the 30-day proposal period expires, submit Form RC532 (Administrative Review Form) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director to review whether due process was followed and whether the review complied with SR&ED law and policy).

body.text: Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has 90 days to file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch (with up to a 1-year extension window if the 90-day deadline was missed; large corporations with >$10 million in taxable capital must pay 50% of the disputed amount). Following a Notice of Confirmation from Appeals, the claimant may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada under either the Informal Procedure (where the disputed amount is limited to $25,000) or the General Procedure (unlimited amounts), with further appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal.
7. Judicial Precedents, Case Law Evolution, and Audit Defence Strategy
7.1 The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998)

The cornerstone of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence is Chief Justice Bowman's decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839). The Tax Court established five cumulative criteria to determine whether claimed activities constitute SR&ED:

items: Criterion 1 (Technological Risk or Uncertainty): Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? (Includes "system uncertainty" where known components interact unpredictably within an integrated system).

Criterion 2 (Hypothesis Formulation): Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? (Entails observing the problem, formulating a clear objective, articulating the uncertainty, formulating a hypothesis, and methodically testing it).
Criterion 3 (Scientific Method): Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses?.

Criterion 4 (Technological Advancement): Did the process result in a technological advancement? (As confirmed in Northwest Hydraulic and Rainbow Pipeline, 96-4369-IT-G, 1999, the rejection of a hypothesis is itself an advancement).
Criterion 5 (Detailed Contemporaneous Record): Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?.

body.text: 7.2 CRA's 2021 "Why and How" Guidelines vs. Binding Appellate Law

In August 2021, the CRA archived its 2015 Eligibility of Work Policy and introduced the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, framing eligibility around two administrative requirements: the "Why" requirement (conducting work to achieve scientific or technological advancement by generating conceptual knowledge rather than mere factual data to resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty) and the "How" requirement (carrying out a systematic investigation or search by generating a hypothesis, testing it by experiment or analysis, developing logical conclusions, and keeping evidence as the work progresses).

However, the Federal Court of Appeal has consistently confirmed—in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 5087, 1998), C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393), Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 FCA 355), R&D Pro-innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016 FCA 152), Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88), National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), and Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada (2026 FCA 175)—that the five criteria from Northwest Hydraulic remain the binding legal test for interpreting subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act.
7.3 Deep Analysis of Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence (1988–2026)

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2019 TCC 246, aff'd 2021 FCA 88), the appellant argued that because the definition of SR&ED had been moved from the Regulations to subsection 248(1) of the ITA and did not explicitly contain the words "scientific method," the Tax Court erred in applying Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic. Applying the Supreme Court of Canada's textual, contextual, and purposive interpretation principles from Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada (2005 SCC 54), the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal with costs fixed at $1,670, holding that Northwest Hydraulic and its appellate progeny remain binding law.

Similarly, in National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2020 TCC 47, aff'd 2022 FCA 72), the Tax Court found that the taxpayer satisfied only Criterion 1 (technological uncertainty) and failed Criteria 2 through 5. The Federal Court of Appeal upheld the denial and affirmed the exclusion of the taxpayer's proposed expert witness because the taxpayer had written 65% of the expert's report, the report acted as an advocate rather than an independent assistant to the court, and the report improperly opined on how domestic law applied to the facts. The FCA also rejected the appellant's attempt to introduce an unproven distinction between the "scientific method" and an "engineering method".

Regarding contemporaneous documentation (Criterion 5), while the courts in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA)), Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313), and Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 42) confirmed that documentary evidence is not strictly mandatory if credible witness testimony establishes all five criteria globally, the Federal Court of Appeal's recent ruling in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada (2025 TCC 183, aff'd 2026 FCA 175, decided October 21, 2026) underscores the fatal risk of poor documentation. In Tuna Temple, despite a credible witness, the taxpayer lost its appeal across 13 food-processing projects (2005–2009) because the work relied on trial-and-error batch adjustments and reconstructed narratives without systematic records of hypothesis testing, and wages were estimated and split evenly across batches.

Conversely, recent Tax Court decisions between 2024 and 2026 demonstrate how taxpayers win when system-level uncertainties and measurable observations are properly documented. In Dazzm Inc. v. The King (2024 TCC 129), the Tax Court allowed a software SR&ED claim involving systemic uncertainties in integrating open-source tools (React and Redux) into a cloud SaaS architecture. In Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC, Docket 2023-2126(IT)I, decided January 17, 2025), Justice Bodie allowed a food-science claim for "Chrisoda" (a shelf-stable cold-pressed beverage where microbial growth initially caused cans to explode), holding that technological uncertainty can exist even when known methods exist in general literature if they have never been used in the specific context, and that practical lab records of pH and microbial counts satisfy Criterion 5. In Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King (2026 TCC 7), the Tax Court issued a split decision—allowing the MTCLM SIL-4 train-control project based on cumulative "system uncertainty," while disallowing $1,293,692 for the SCADACOM-5 upgrade because modernizing and scaling software with known tools is routine product development. Finally, in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173), the Tax Court held that plagiarized supplier/website text in technical SR&ED reports constituted a misrepresentation that reopened statute-barred years and supported section 163(2) penalties.

body.text: 7.5 Contemporaneous Documentation Checklist for Audit Readiness

To satisfy Criterion 5 of Northwest Hydraulic and the CRA's April 20, 2026 SR&ED Review Process Guide, claimants must maintain contemporaneous evidence generated at the time the work was carried out establishing what work was done, who was involved, and when the work took place:

items: Project Planning and Hypothesis Records: Project planning documents, experimental plans, design of experiments, system architecture documents, and technical drawings articulating the specific scientific or technological uncertainty.

Iterative Testing and Analytical Logs: Dated laboratory notebooks, source code repositories, records of trial runs, test protocols, measurable test data (e.g., benchmark metrics, pH/microbial counts), analysis, and conclusions showing how hypotheses evolved.
Physical and Visual Artifacts: Dated photographs, videos, physical prototypes, samples, and scrap/destruction records supporting materials consumed vs. transformed.

Contemporaneous Labour and Time Tracking: Real-time timesheets, activity records, and payroll ledgers linking specific employees to specific SR&ED projects (avoiding retroactive estimates rejected in Tuna Temple), alongside timely filed Form T1174 and Schedule 49.

Financial, Subcontractor, and Capital Equipment Records: General ledgers, purchase invoices, proof of payment within the taxation year (or within 180 days for wages under subsection 78(4)), signed Canadian subcontractor statements of work, Form T1263 for third-party payments, and machine operating-time logbooks supporting post-December 15, 2024 ASA capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (Boxes 788–796 of Form T661), and leased equipment.
